utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Would you please call the case, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before I give you the opportunity, Mr. Emmerson, to continue your cross-examination, two small matters. There is a request by the Prosecution to send a letter with corrections to Professor Aleksandric. Before the Chamber decides this matter, the Chamber would like to know whether there's any objection by the Defence. I see "no," by Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey? Then second, the Chamber was informed that the Haradinaj and Balaj Defence do not oppose a request for protective measures for the witness who's scheduled for tomorrow. The Chamber would like to know, Mr. Harvey, what your position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I apologise that the information didn't get through to the Court. We also have no objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. I don't know whether you have to apologise or whether it was our fault. We just don't know. But it's on the record now that all three Defence teams do not object. Then good morning -- good morning, Mr. Stijovic. May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. Emmerson will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Emmerson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could be given the black binder, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think he has it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He has it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, could you turn to tab 14, please. I have just one or two further questions to ask you about your interview with Radomir Markovic and the testimony you gave in the Milosevic trial. First of all, tab number 14, can I ask you, please, to identify that document and your signature on it, the statement that was taken from Mr. Markovic on the 26th of June, 2001.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May that please be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be marked for identification as D171.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I should also ask at the same time that the briefing note which is behind tab 13 be marked for identification as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be marked for identification as D172.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution will be taking an objection at the appropriate time to the admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Especially --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's good to know it's on the record. We'll consider that when it comes to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, as regards this statement, Mr. Stijovic, we can see in the English translation on page 1 about ten lines down, the sentence beginning: "Beyond the main topic of the meeting," where you refer -- or, I'm sorry, where the statement refers to the content of a meeting that took place in March 1999 at which Mr. Markovic was present together with President Milosevic, Mr. Stojiljkovic, and Vlastimir Djordjevic. I'll just read a short passage into the record, if I may. "Beyond the main topic of the meeting, at its very end, Vlastimir Djordjevic raised the problem of removing Albanian bodies to remove all possible civilian victims who could become the subject of an investigation by The Hague Tribunal. Mr. Milosevic ordered Vlajko Stojiljkovic to undertake the measures necessary to remove the bodies of the Albanian citizens who had already been buried. I personally did not get involved in the conversation on this topic, since none of the orders was directed at me." "I know that Stojiljkovic appointed General Dragan Ilic to implement this task and that the latter then went with a specific team of collaborators to the KIM area. I personally did not want to allow the RDB to get involved in this morbid tale of later disinterment and removal of the bodies, so as far as I know, it was the RJB and members of the VJ that participated in this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm ending the quotation at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, were those the words of Radomir Markovic or -- or were they words that you, so to speak, put into his mouth?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interrogated Radomir Markovic to the best of my knowledge about the events in Kosovo and Metohija and on the basis of the task given to me from the leadership of the State Security Service. This is -- these are the words of Radomir Markovic, the way he uttered them, and I relayed them in his statement. These are his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, part of your reading was about Albanian citizens who had already been buried, where I see in the original "civilians."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The distinction is not -- it was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I apologise. It was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll turn into private session, if that's what -- yes. We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Having dealt with the -- the top end of the organisation, I want to now look at the -- the grassroots end, if I can put it that way. I'm going to just read to you a sentence from a statement made by your boss, David Gajic, chief of RDB in Kosovo, where he refers to some information. This is not in evidence, this statement, although Your Honours have seen it before. It is statement made in August 2003 to the Office of the Prosecutor commenting on the Joint Command minutes. And he refers at one stage, Mr. Stijovic, in the statement to an entry in the minutes of the Joint Command, which is an entry recording something that he had said. And he says: "This information was provided to the RDB by the head of our local office, Vule Mrksic is V-u-l-e Mrksic. . Now, can I ask you, please: Who is Vule Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A person by that name was not part of the State Security Service. David Gajic is dead. He passed away a year or two. Just to inform the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anybody by the name of Vule Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you know anybody by the name of Vukmir Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the Vladimir Mrksic that you've told us about, an operative working in the Decane office of the DB, Vladimir Mrksic, did he have a shortened version of his name at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, there seems to be a misunderstanding there. Not Vladimir Mrksic. Rather, Vladimir Mircic. And I pronounced his name that way. There is no Vladimir Mrksic, only Vladimir Mircic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Then we may have a translation problem. The passage from Mr. Gajic's statement refers to Vule Mircic, M-i-r-c-i-c. Now, did Vladimir Mircic that you've told us about in Decane go by the name of Vule or Vula?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't have the correct information. Let me tell you this correctly. Vladimir Mircic is an operative of State Security in Decani. Vukmir Mircic, aka Vula is his brother, and he was the chief of MUP Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Correction: The chief of OUP Decani.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are probably the persons you're talking about. When we were in private session, I was explaining that signature, you'll recall, and the -- and he was not the -- the second signature but the third signature. I said that I recognised his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to that signature in a -- in a moment or two. So that is Vladimir Mircic and his brother is Vula or Vukmir Mircic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I constantly receive in my translation Mrksic. It's not Mrksic. It's Mircic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We receive on our transcript -- we receive Mircic as the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's how -- also how I hear Mr. Emmerson pronounce the name. So from now on, unless we get notice, it is Mircic we are talking about, two brothers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And again, so that we're clear, Vladimir was an official of the RDB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And where was he based?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the building of the Decani OUP -- or rather, Decani SUP in the town of Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And Vule or Vula, you say he was not a member of the RDB or he was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't a member of the RDB. He was chief of the Decani OUP. That's organ of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So the two brothers worked together in the same building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you about a number of documents now. First of all, could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your last question was a composite question. It could be that -- but there is a risk in the same building and working together is not the same place or working together -- "working together," I would like to have that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The two brothers were based in the same building in Deqan for the purposes of their respective work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, they were based in the same building, but they didn't do the same jobs. The older brother was in the department of the public security and the younger brother was in the department of state security. And these are two different domains. However, they were sitting in the same building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very often when people were brought into custody, they would be interrogated first by public security officers and then by state security officers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not correct. It depended on the particular job that the person had.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Just -- just to be clear, I mean, we've seen at least one example of it already in this case. People were -- people taken into custody were interviewed by both organs on occasions, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And they'd be sharing information and effectively working side by side; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The public security service, if I need to explain, conducted initial interview with the person brought in. However, if through the information obtained from this individual there was some interest for the State Security Service, then the State Security Service would continue the interview about the circumstances, because the State Security Service had good quality information and they were dealing with terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And in those circumstances, the suspect would be taken to the fourth floor, is that right, of the Deqani police station for interrogation by the RDB?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the way. First of all, there were no floors in that building. The second floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. You're sure -- sure about that, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Correction: It didn't have four floors.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Forgive me, but we've heard testimony from people who have worked there who said that it did and that's where the RDB was based. Is that possibly your recollection at fault, then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had -- that they were taken to the fourth floor? I'm absolutely certain about my memory. There was no fourth floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All right. Very well. I'll -- it's conceivable that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they taken to the floor where the RDB was working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the second floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It could be an error on my part. I'll check the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the fourth floor was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we please turn to tab 23 for a moment in the bundle. And as I ask you to do that, Mr. Stijovic, I -- I want to ask you this: Did you ever learn of complaints that people who had been taken into custody at Gjakova or Deqan police station or indeed Pec were mistreated by the RDB or RJB, public security or state security? They were beaten?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received this information subsequently, most often when the trial was already in progress, and that happened at the main hearing. The individuals were then denied the statements that they had given, claiming that they had been taken under duress and with the use of violence against them during examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, let's look at tab 23 for a moment, because that's not a statement that was made at trial but a statement that was made by an individual three days after the statement that you have annexed as annex 41 to your witness statement. Now, annex 41 is one of those in respect of which the Trial Chamber has indicated that it is in the territory of potential non-admission, but if you remind yourself of annex 41 to your witness statement, which is marked for identification P973, that is a statement allegedly made by somebody called Rifat or -- Haradinaj, a record compiled of an interview allegedly by somebody called Rifat Haradinaj and dated the 27th of March dealing with events of the 24th and 25th of March. If we could turn to tab 23, then, for a moment. This is, for the record, a part of Exhibit P5 -- it's already in evidence. It's Exhibit P5, page 30. Now, this is a statement taken from the same gentleman three days later, on the 30th of March, by an organisation called the Humanitarian Law Centre. And if we look at the substance of the statement, he refers to having been arrested on the 24th of March at some distance from the Haradinaj family compound, and it indicates that he had not himself witnessed the exchange of fire around the compound itself. And then in the third paragraph of his statement, he says this following his arrest: "They -- then they took us to Eljmi's house where the attack was and knocked us down onto the sand. There were 10 or 11 of us. I don't know exactly, because I didn't raise -- dare raise my head to see. Us four were among the first. The others were brought in later. We lay there for a long time. They stomped on our backs, heads, and legs and hit us with their rifle butts. They drove the Pinzgauer up very close, like they were going to run over us. They said they would slit our throats, shoot us. Then the one in charge came up and told them to stop it." "Later on they took us off the street and into Dragoslav's yard, because foreign reporters were coming. They didn't beat us in the yard, just handcuffed us. At about half past 8.00, they put us in a car and drove to Gjakova. There were two bodies lying near the steps at the police station there. They lined us up and told us to identify them. I couldn't, because they were badly shot up. I could hardly stay upright because of the beating I'd got. They beat an old man. And when I looked in that direction, they got mad and began hitting me again." "It was one after midnight when the questioning started. The inspectors asked me how the attack began and what I knew about the UCK. They questioned me the next day too. They made me say in front of a camera that what Dragoslav Stojanovic had said about his house being fired at from Eljmi's house was true. In the beginning I told the truth - that I couldn't see if there was shooting from Elmji's house because mine is two kilometres away. But they finally made me say Dragoslav's statement was true. They let me go at 3.30 in the afternoon on the 26th of March." That is the -- the statement as it appears. And then the record that you have, which is unsigned, at annex 41 of this interrogation is dated the following day, the 27th of March, the day after this interview took place. Now, Mr. Stijovic, people were beaten, weren't they, in custody routinely, both by officers of the RJB and by officers of the RDB? And you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What you have just read out, Your Honours, I may comment upon and I can do it on each sentence uttered by this person in the statement given to the Humanitarian Law Centre. But what I would like to do and what I would like everybody to do, to put this in the context and the time and the events. As concerning the use of violence, these things probably occurred. I cannot say that it was not the case, and I don't think there is any police force in the world not using these methods at least at one point when they overstep the boundaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You weren't there during this interrogation, were you, Mr. Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. But a good friend of mine, Mr. Otovic, was killed on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We are aware of that. You mentioned earlier on a statement that was discussed in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So could we just go in very briefly to private session to identify the statement concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: For clarity sake, you identified the signature at the bottom of the statement, annex 18, as Vukmir Mircic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not correct. I also said then, when this was shown to me, that it was Vladimir Mircic. I remember well. And you can look at the annex shown to me by the Prosecution that his signature was the second or the third one and that I recognised it. It was Vladimir Mircic, and that is when I said that this was probably him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You're quite correct. I misspoke myself. If we could just look, please, behind tab 24. There is here a statement which was taken, as you can see, on the 6th of October, that is, two days before you testified about annex 18. It is the same of Muhamet Avdijai, and the relevant passage reads as follows: "I was arrested by the police in Junik on the 19th of February, 1998. I was taken to the police station in Junik, where for the next three hours I was repeatedly beaten by the police. They used their plastic batons to beat me, as well as their fists and feet. After around three hours, other police arrived at the station in Junik. They were from Decan. They took me from Junik to the police station in Decan, where for the next two or three hours they carried on with the same treatment as the police in Junik. I was beaten in the same manner." "I do recall meeting a man there, one of the police officers, who I knew as Vula Mircic. It was in his office that I was interviewed between being beaten. After around three hours, officers from the UDB arrived there. They took me to the police station in Peja. I was repeatedly beaten there by them. They interviewed me in between the beatings, but I was in no condition to know what I was being asked. I do not remember what I was asked exactly. I do not remember signing any statement there, but I was later taken to court in Peja where -- where one was produced. I refused to accept the allegations being made about me and no witnesses were ever called to the court to give evidence. "I can say that during the time that I was being interviewed I was told things by the people interviewing me and asked to agree them -- agree with them. I never volunteered anything myself. I have never voluntarily given any statement to the Serbian authorities about anything that was happening in Kosovo in 1998. "I just wish to clarify what I mean by the police in Peja. At the police station there were also offices of the UDB and it was in their offices that I was interviewed, by them, not the usual police, and it was at their hands that I was beaten." Mr. Stijovic, are you in a position to contradict that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me, Your Honours, to explain this, because this was a lengthy quotation and I cannot just give a yes or a no answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please explain what you'd like to explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I am talking here about things to the best of my knowledge, and I continue to do so. I express some suspicion about this hindsight, especially referring to the statement taken on the 6th of October, 2006 -- correction, 2007, that refer to the events that took years ago. And I mentioned that there was a method that statements were given to the organs of the police and to the investigators which were later denied in court. In this particular instance, the gentleman you mentioned had an opportunity to point out to the court in Pec, when he was brought in -- or draw their attention that violence or any illegal methods were applied to him. And this would have been responded to by the court. It seems to me that he failed to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: On what do you base that observation? Did you -- do you study the court records, Mr. Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't studied the court records, but we used the court records as a kind of guidance in our operation in our department. And I believe that the court decisions are -- were very important both in the past and in the future for our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps in -- in order to -- perhaps to shortcut matters, of course, looking at these statements now opens several possibilities, of course, which Mr. Emmerson is now exploring. The one is that those who have taken the statements might not easily acknowledge that they were recorded in a false manner and that they reflected what was not said. But there's also another possibility, that is, that those who gave the statements at the time have difficulties in acknowledging what they said at the time. So these two poles, to say so, is -- are, of course,-- the Chamber is well aware of that. To the extent we can clarify it, whether we can establish whether it was the one or the other, that's fine. The Chamber is not over-optimistic in this respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But to be absolutely clear about it, Mr. Stijovic, you testified on Monday that not only were you not present at these interrogations but that the extent of your knowledge was having read the two documents that are in -- annexed as annexes 17 and 18; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as these two statements that were shown to me are concerned, yes. Time-wise, I was in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you turn to tab 21, please, for a moment. Tab 21 is not yet marked for identification. It is Defence document 1D00-1793, and the translation of this document is a draft translation. Might it be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will marked for identification as D173.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to explain this document to you before I ask you about it -- the contents, Mr. Stijovic, this is a document filed with the Peja district court in November 2001, based on an investigation conducted by the council for the defence of human rights and freedoms in Kosovo and statements taken from Albanian citizens about alleged crimes committed by Serb forces and Serb officials. And this document is a complaint against Vukmir Mircic? Now, just to help us, if you can, to -- to compare the biographical information. It indicates that "Vukmir Mircic, known from his mother, Vasilika, and father Mitar, with the name Vula, born on September 11, 1954 in the village of Kodrali." Are those biographical details correct, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly cannot tell you his date of birth, but that Vukmir Mircic was what it says here, that's true. As far as his mother's name or which school he finished, I really cannot be of any help in that department.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We can see a little later further down he used to work in the municipal court of Deqan as a typist, a job he switched with the Serbian internal affairs UDB job in Peje. Moreover, he was also a chief of Serbian place in Deqan. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you're putting this document to the witness. Wouldn't we first ask whether he knows anything about the existence of the document or about the content of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then perhaps go -- ask him whether he was aware that the council for the defence of human rights and freedoms lodged a complaint against Mr. Mircic, and then we would know whether it makes any sense at all to put further questions to him in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: First of all, were you aware that a formal complaint had been lodged against Mr. Mircic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going, if I may, nonetheless to ask you one or two supplementary questions in relation to the content. If we turn to paragraph 5, for example, many of the allegations relate to crimes allegedly committed in 1999. But the paragraph 5 records an allegation that in June 1998, Mr. Mircic came to the house of the man called Qazim Bid Kuqit in Decan and took 15 immobilised civilian population to the police station in Decan, torturing them and beating them for two days and nights. After two days, 14 of them were released. While on the other side, they held Beqir Regje Cacaj for another two days and nights torturing. Afterwards, he got released in very bad health conditions. Therefore, he died after two days and in his last minutes of life was saying, "I'm dying because of Vula." Now, do any of those names mean anything to you, Mr. Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they don't mean anything to me. But it's simply illogical to me that one man can take away 15 immobilised persons. That would require a huge amount of logistics, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not, where there's no personal knowledge of the event, start speculating on whether he was alone or with a group and whether -- we haven't seen the -- any statement of the witness. It's just a summary, Mr. Emmerson. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you ever investigate complaints about ill-treatment by RDB or RJB officials?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this testimony, I cannot tell you exactly when, but you will find it easily - said that I headed and organised the collection of evidence pertaining to the crimes committed in Kosovo and Metohija and that these involved the activities or crimes committed both by the Albanians, i.e., members of the KLA and FARK, and the Serbs, members of the police, soldiers, and civilians. So this involved crimes. We compiled documentation with the aim and intention to hand over these documents to the competent judicial organs for further processing. So in response to your question, my answer is "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, was anybody ever prosecuted in respect of interrogations conducted by RDB officials?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you, and I can explain you the reasons why I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If it would be helpful to explain the reasons, then please do; otherwise ...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early January, I fell quite ill. I had heart problems and I was sent for treatment to Belgrade, and I never returned back until March, the start of bombardment. Other people were involved in that. Then the bombing started. I interrupted my treatment of my own accord. I then continued my treatment. And from 1999 to 2003, I was involved in business that had nothing to do with Albanian terrorism and these activities, so that I did not have access to the documentation concerning the crimes committed in Kosovo and Metohija in that period of time both by Serbs and Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. And you have no independent knowledge one way or the other whether any proceedings were brought against RDB officials, I mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. I want to turn to another topic that you mentioned in your testimony yesterday, and that was the ambush, as you described it, on the 28th of February, 1998 in Likoshan, where you said that following the ambush search operations were conducted in Likoshan and the villages around it. Can I be clear what you mean by "search operations," please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The searches meant looking after, tracking down the attackers who opened fire on the police. They were on the hunt after them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And can I ask you this before looking at Likoshan in a bit more detail: On the 5th of March, there was a police operation on the Jashari compound in Prekaze. Was that also what you would characterise as a search operation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not a search operation. That was an attempt at arresting Adem Jashari and his group.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. In the course of the search operation in and around Likoshan and the arrest operation in Prekaze on the 5th of March, can you tell us, please, what investigations were conducted into crimes allegedly committed by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, some intelligence was obtained - and I'm telling you this to the best of my knowledge. There is ongoing work on these matters since in Belgrade there exists a special chamber with the Belgrade district court, this chamber for war crimes, and there is a separate prosecutor's office for war crimes. All the information indicating or pointing to such activities was forwarded to these offices. And as far as I know, there is an ongoing investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. And an ongoing investigation still, nine years later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, that is the answer of the witness. You are more or less --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- trying to ask his comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You seem to have, if I may say so, rather a lot of knowledge of the detail of what was going in and around Likoshan at that time, because you've testified about the KLA ambush and other matters of that nature. Were crimes committed, as far as you know, by Serb forces in Likoshan and Prekaze?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were many victims. I know that we carried out certain activities to investigate all the circumstances leading to that incident. I know that there is still work being done on that, just as we are dealing today still here with crimes committed in Kosovo nine years ago. And I apologise, Your Honours, if you deem this last remark of mine improper.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Correction: Crimes committed by the KLA in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to be clear, another Chamber of this Court has found that the -- the evidence is that 83 Kosovar Albanians were killed in those operations, including elderly people, and at least 24 women and children, that a pregnant woman was shot in the face and a baby killed in Prekaze. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is there a reference to a judgement of the Trial Chamber or --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. It is the Limaj judgement, paragraph 49. I wasn't going to read the whole paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We've also heard testimony from Colonel Crosland, who visited the Prekaze site, that bodies appeared to have been shot at close range and, as the Limaj Trial Chamber found at paragraph 49, there were reports of summary executions. Is this information that you investigated at the time, Mr. Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before the witness answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My recollection is that this matter was not adjudicated by the Limaj -- the Limaj Trial Chamber. It was a matter which is referred to as historical events leading up to the matters which were in the Limaj indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would -- I would tend to disagree. That was -- this was evidence that was introduced during the Limaj trial and evidence upon which the Limaj Chamber made its determination and its judgement, and these were adjudicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It was outside the indictment period. It was before the indictment -- Limaj indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, sometimes facts are established in a judgement even if they are not part of the indictment. At the same time, we should be very cautious, because the Defence might be focusing less on facts that are not in the core of the indictment. So to that extent, some caution --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I can certainly help find the passage over the break. But the Prosecution itself makes the same allegations in very much the same terms in the Milutinovic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But still to be proven, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Still to be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Let's -- perhaps, Mr. Emmerson, if you go into less details about it, but we could ask the witness whether, in view of these facts, whether he considers that these allegations have been sufficiently investigated at the time, if at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, these allegations are still being investigated into, and a good many of these allegations were confirmed. And I repeat, I am speaking to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, you told us that it was your responsibility at the time to investigate crimes committed in Kosovo in the context of this conflict. Can you help us, please, what steps did you take to investigate these two incidents? That is, before the change of regime in Belgrade. What steps did you take?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to recount the entire procedure under which we worked?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I would like you to tell us in very summary form what steps you personally took to investigate war crimes committed by Serbian forces in Likoshan and Prekaze, please, in 1998. In other words, what steps you took at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, I think Mr. Emmerson is mainly interested to know whether you paid serious attention to crimes committed by Serbian forces at the time or whether you were not much interested in investigating them and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a highly serious manner. In a highly serious manner. Because the consequences of these events, the repercussions of these events were great for the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then tell us exactly in relation to the two incidents mentioned what you investigated or what you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically within my sector in -- where I worked and which I directed, we produced a plan of work for these matters. And in relation to this case as well as for all the other cases where there were indications that there were war crimes committed, a dossier was formed through public security which was duty-bound by the law to conduct a scene of crime investigation. This was out of our jurisdiction. We weren't involved in that. That's why we obtained information from public security on these events. On the other hand, other sources were the Albanian media who reported on some of the information that we had obtained through operative work. Next followed the interviewing of persons who could help clarify these events. For every case where there were indications that they involved a war crime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer -- your answers now strike me as being of a rather general nature. If -- if any such thing happened, I'd like to hear from you that the day after the Likoshan operation I tasked Mr. X, Y, or Z to interrogate allegations that 20 people were killed... I'd like to have concrete answers to those questions, rather than that you were duty-bound to start a file and that a work plan was made, because without being cynical, it -- it happens in this world that work plans are made mainly for the purpose of not performing the -- the work. I'm not saying that that was the case, but I'd like to receive concrete information about what you actually did. Or what was done under your responsibility. Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I do apologise for interrupting. I have to leave the room for a brief spell. There's no objection -- and thus leave my client without counsel at the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: But there's no objection to matters continuing in my absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: With your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll miss him -- Mr. Troop, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: He'll be back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr -- or I would like to ask the witness first to answer a question: Could you give us concrete information. I formed a team of five people consisting of A, B, C, D, and E which I sent to the location the week after that or I sent someone to the investigating judge and asking for his assistance and -- whatever, but rather concrete information than general statements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. I did not have operative authorities enabling me to conduct an investigation in the sense of the criminal law. What was within my ambit was to collect the documentation that was relevant for that. The analysis department asked from operative leaders and persons working on the ground to send all the information they had in order to have a compilation of the relevant documentation in one spot. I have to tell you, unfortunately, that many people in the police and the state security service underestimated the significance of a timely and active effort in the exercise to clarify the events on both sides, and perhaps that lay at the heart of the problem that the efforts at collecting documentation for Kosovo encountered. I did the best I could, given the position that I occupied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I try to understand your answer that you said we're asking for information but we didn't receive it in a timely manner. And then how much did you insist? How often did you repeat your request? And what measures you took in order to receive that information? And when, finally, did you receive it, if you received it at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documentation arrived quite slowly. And I mean the documentation about the incidents down there and about the events in general. And I have to tell you that one of the reasons why I ended up ill in the end was the terrible stress and the terrible pressure in trying to -- to explain the significance of this process to the people who were involved in the job. The persons heading these departments were not forthcoming in that process. My analysts and people working on the documentation were the ones who were sitting in the building and who were supposed to make an analysis of these events, to make an assessment of these events. These were not operatives who would have the authority to go out into the field, investigate people, and investigate these events. And that's all I can tell you on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for your information, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, the Chamber gained sufficient impression on the activities developed at that time, which might also explain the nine-year period. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I move on to another topic, please, Mr. Stijovic. In the period running up to 1998 and specifically during 1997, did you meet a man called Mahmut Bakalli in Prishtine?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did you also meet at the same time a man called Baton Haxhiu?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to gather this from the transcript. You're probably referring to Baton Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you turn to tab 17 in the bundle, please. This is a statement tendered by the Prosecution under Rule 92 bis both in the Milosevic and in the Milutinovic trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll ask that it please be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, tab 17 is document ID 1D62-0029. It will be marked for identification as D174.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to pick it up, if I may, please, on page 7, in the numbers in the bottom right-hand corner. I don't think you -- you -- well, perhaps I should ask you. Do you read English, Mr. Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But you do read Albanian.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the sake of the Trial Chamber, I believe it would be better for me to have this interpreted into Serbian. I do read Albanian, but I do hesitate to get the information this way, because I might get something wrong. I -- I'd rather have the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, it's my error, the -- I'd assumed the translation was Albanian without checking it. In fact, it is a Serbian translation, which you have immediately behind the English. And the passage that I'm going to begin with is on page 5 of the Serbian, and it's the -- starts at the third paragraph on page 5, and it continues to the fourth paragraph on page 6. I'm going to put a specific passage to you in just a moment, but if I can simply summarise the background to this. Mr. Bakalli in this statement describes a meeting in November 1997 at which you had arranged via a telephone call to him for discussions between the Serbian side and the Albanian side about respective demands for autonomy for Kosovo and independence for Kosovo. And he describes the meeting as having taken place in Mr. Bakalli's apartment on a Saturday in Prishtine. And he indicates that the Albanian side was represented by Mr. Bakalli and himself and the Serbian delegation consisted of yourself, David Gajic, Jovica Stanisic, as well as a man he thinks was called Hadic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I apologise. I think this is an error where it says that I spoke over the phone with Bakalli. As far as I'm able to glean from this -- it's line 24, I think. "Bakalli in this statement describes --"

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're absolutely right. It's -- again, I misspoke myself. It's Mr. Haxhiu who describes the meeting between himself and Mr. Bakalli on one hand, and yourself, Mr. Gajic, Mr. Stanisic, and another man on the other hand. Do you remember the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And without going into the details of what was put forward by Mr. Bakalli, the statement describes the Albanian position as being set out in effect as greater autonomy but something short of full independence. And I'm looking now in the English on page 7 and in the Serbian on page 6. And I'm looking at the third full paragraph on page 6 in the Serbian and the first paragraph on page 7 in the English. And it reads as follows: "Gajic then responded to Bakalli's proposal. He said that if Bakalli's presentation was the Albanians' final proposal, then the negotiations were over. The Serbs will never accept this, he said. If you insist on this, Gajic said, then Kosovo is in great danger. I responded that I didn't think Albanians would accept anything less. Gajic said if this was our final position, then it meant war." He goes on: "I don't remember exactly which members of the Serbian delegation said what, because we were all discussing back and forth. But I am certain of one of them -- I am certain that one of them, I believe it was Hadic, said that the Serbian forces were very strong. There is a plan" -- and my pronunciation will no doubt be wrong here. "There is a plan called Sprzena Zemlja, he said, and this can be implemented within 24 hours. In English, this could be translated into 'burnt land' or 'scorched earth'. Stijovic, I believe, said that this military plan of action was in the mind of many Serbs. I remember that one of them said there are 463 ethnic Albanian villages in Kosovo - maybe he said 643 - and they will all be burned. I believe Gajic said that." Can I ask you, please, to comment on that passage that I just read to you, Mr. Stijovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can comment on it, but I would like Their Honours to permit me to give you a brief answer. I know that I've been asked not to go into details, but I'd like the permission to explain as briefly as possible the events concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, before -- before you do, were those words spoken by somebody in the Serbian delegation referring to a scorched earth policy and the burning of a -- a number of hundred Albanian villages?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us, please, what explanation you'd like to give.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have always been the sort of person open to dialogue and discussion and I tried to ensure that the situation, the developments in Kosovo and Metohija, took as normal a course as possible. In that context in late 1997, a meeting was held in the flat of Mahmut Bakalli in Prishtine, which was attended by the late Bakalli, journalist Baton Haxhiu, David Gajic, the then-assistant chief of the DB, the assistant to Jovica Stanisic, and Milosav Vilotic, assistant chief of the DB of Serbia. Therefore, there was no Hadzic person who attended the meeting. What Bakalli said at the time and what you relayed here as greater autonomy but something short of independence, well, it wasn't really along those lines. This is what Bakalli said, and I will refer you to the following meeting that was held in Brezovica, which was video and audio recorded. Bakalli said that the KLA activities had gone so far that general armed conflicts could quite easily break out in Kosovo and Metohija. He said that it was the last ditch attempt for the politicians and the politics to try and prevent the spread of clashes that were imminently to come, and this he proved to be quite foreseeable in that. He said that through the State Security Service a message should be sent to Milosevic that the Albanians and Serbs should engage in discussions about -- for a final solution of Kosovo and Metohija because the KLA was just a part of the problem in Kosovo and Metohija. And Bakalli stated this proposal, which enjoyed the support of all the politicians, and that was Kosovo and Metohija outside the legal jurisdiction of Serbia but within Yugoslavia without a border toward Serbia but with an established border toward Albania and Macedonia. This was in compliance with all the principles coming from the Dayton Accords and the principles espoused by the International Community. This conversation in Bakalli's flat was the sort of conversation which made it possible after a while, as a special envoy of President Milosevic, Jovica Stanisic met with Bakalli in a building of ours in Brezovica, and this meeting was recorded. There is a video and audio recording. Bakalli, I, and another person - the witness mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not attend this meeting. Baton Haxhiu testified about this meeting as did Bakalli. Upon his arrival, Baton Haxhiu gave an interview, an extensive interview, where he minimised the role of the meetings and presented a host of elements that did not result from these meetings. Baton Haxhiu is an acquaintance of mine, a good journalist, and I did not want in any way to be detrimental to him, to make any problems to him. Bakalli, after the testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you there. We're talking about a meeting which apparently has taken place in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The -- the perception of what happened during that meeting seems to be quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't seek to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One seems to be more inclined to play the peace-seeking party oneself and to blame the other party. I mean, that's -- it's not the core of this case. I think you've drawn our attention to something where the witness said the report about what happened is not correct. I've got a different memory on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I have very little further for this witness. But may we take the break at this point so that I can review what -- what further questions I need to deal with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. Stijovic, I do understand that you'd like to explain your position in -- in some detail. Often if you say those words were not spoken, it was rather we who wanted to seek resolutions for the matter, it was the other party which -- then we don't have to go in that much detail of what really is not the core of this case. We'll have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, before you continue, is there any doubt in your mind as that the Defence - I'm also addressing other Defence counsel - that we could finish the witness well in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I have about 15 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe, based on the examinations that have occurred thus far, coupled with some of the comments that have been made by the Chamber, that we will finish well within time. I'm changing part of my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Reducing detail, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I have also been listening very carefully about the comments that have followed about Your Honours' lips about what may or may not be relevant and I should be cutting my cross accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Re, re-examination will then, in view of what has just been said, not take that much time that the witness could not leave in time. Yes. I would say nodding is not on the record. But you're nodding yes, Mr. Re. It's now on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's hard not to nod.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Mr. Emmerson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I just correct one matter in respect of which I misspoke myself earlier on, and it relates to the four floors/two floors issue. In fact, the testimony is that it was the police station in Gjakova had four floors, rather than the police station in Deqan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So to that extent, I correct the question that I put earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That was at page 6201 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the evidence. I only said --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- there was a fourth floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But in a different location. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, I gather from the testimony that you gave last week that there were individuals who were in fact cooperating with your service but who were continuing to be active members of the KLA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you told us that amongst one of the motives that might persuade them to cooperate was the giving effectively of an immunity to them for alleged criminal activity up until that point. Can I ask you: Were they given an immunity for any alleged infringements of the criminal law after they were operating as part of your service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So continuing to take part in the activities of the KLA, that would be a crime, would it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Activities in the KLA, such as murders, theft of property, and the like, we were not prepared to grant immunities to our associates. And they were aware of that. They were guided in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to be clear, simple membership of the KLA at this time was a crime, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not a crime. The very fact that somebody was a member of the KLA, that was a hostile activity; however, a crime is something that is being committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So, for example, if the KLA or -- including one of your agents were to launch a military attack on a police unit and to shoot and kill police officers, armed police officers, in the course of such an attack, would that be a crime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you're entering an area which is closely linked to the existence of armed conflict, and it could have a lot of legal implications. Your question requires thorough knowledge of legal matters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is a crime -- if you would say whether this was an act which is described in criminal law, that's not exactly the same as a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I -- let me -- let me put the question more precisely, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were your operatives, that is to say, the agents that you had infiltrated or recruited within the KLA, were they given to understand that if they took part in armed engagements with Serbian forces, they would or would not be prosecuted for it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They knew - that is to say, during the training conducted by an operative - were informed that they were not allowed to participate in any activities that might end up as a crime of murder, serious injury, not to mention war crime and other more serious crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you know whether such individuals were ever tasked either by members of your service or by members of the RJB to commit crimes in order to implicate or discredit the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, I can only say what refers to the security service. Definitely no, and they were never given. And I believe that the same applied to the public security services; although, I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you: Do you know or did you know at the time a man called Momir or Miomir Mitic, a police chief in Ferizaj?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you help us with the name at all? You may not have known him, but did you know of him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I don't know. There were over 20.000 policemen in Kosovo. I couldn't have known the names of each and every one.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, the names of the RDB officials in Ferizaj, perhaps starting with the chief of the RDB in Ferizaj, in March 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, the location doesn't ring a bell to me. Could we -- could we try to find out where Ferizaj approximately is.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you give us the approximate location of Ferizaj, please. Am I right in thinking this is broadly speaking, south-east in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Urosevac is the place located on the direction towards Macedonia. I'm not very good at geography. It's about 40 kilometres from Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So Ferizaj is 40 kilometres from Prishtine?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ferizaj is the Albanian name for Urosevac. About 40 kilometres. I cannot give you the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And can you help us, please, as to the names of the senior RDB officials in Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how much this question is something within my capability. I'm afraid that this would constitute or be in contravention of the secrecy, official secrecy obligation. I am not a lawyer, but I am not competent enough to judge whether any discussion about how the organ -- the service or structure was -- be something beyond my authority. I was authorised and I can only speak about the events that took place in Kosovo and Metohija at the time. So this was a secret service. These were operatives of the security service who are still working there. And I think this is an impossible proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, I do not know what the relevance and the importance is of this information, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith is on his feet as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, if I might. In the Milosevic trial, the issue of RDB as well as public officials who were operating at that area was raised by the Prosecution. I believe it was raised both in private and in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, maybe we might just go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And its document identification is 1D62-0096.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If I can summarise the background to this statement, Mr. Stijovic, it -- it describes events that took place very shortly after the incident in Prekaze on the 5th of March in which the maker of this statement describes being called to a meeting in Ferizaj with Momir Mitic, the police chief of Ferizaj, and a man called Jashanin, who is described as having -- and this is page 4, fourth paragraph, pre-penultimate line -- who is described as having joined the police station in 1998, originally coming from Serbia, and was the chief of the -- was the chief of the DB in Ferizaj. And this individual describes having been recruited as an agent at that meeting and being told that he would be issued with a uniform, weapons, and Chinese ammunition, and describes having been taken to Prishtine and introduced to a commander of the SAJ and, in particular, an individual who he was told had been involved in Prekaze. And if I can pick it up at the English at the bottom of page 5, he says that: "At the meeting in Prishtine with the SAJ officer and Mr. Mitic," he was given a number of tasks. And I'll just read these -- this one short paragraph: "Firstly, he said" - that is, Mr. Mitic said - "there is an Albanian man in the village of Manastirc, Ferizaj, who owned a number of buses. He wanted to burn all the buses and leave a note nearby which would say something like 'these buses are never to drive Serbians again'. The letter will have a KLA badge stuck to it. Mitic explained that this would make the owner of the buses and everybody else think that the KLA were responsible for burning the buses. And when Mitic finished explaining the plan, the commander" -- that is, the SAJ commander -- "said, 'this plan is approved.'" And then over the page: "Mitic then continued, saying that he had identified a number of target locations which he wanted to throw grenades at." And he mentioned them one at a time and gave reasons for each; I don't go through them individually. Now, pausing there. First of all, were you aware of any such plan in relation to Ferizaj that agents be recruited to commit crimes in that area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I'm not sure who are you referring to when you said they were recruited by someone. Can you clarify that for me? As far as I know, the State Security Service definitely had nothing to do with this. However, as far as the details relating to these persons mentioned here, they could be more helpful. I see this document for the first time and what you have just said or quoted is something that I also hear for the first time. An imagination is a wonderful thing and it can do wonders.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. In answer to your question as to recruitment, that is spelled out on page 4 in the fourth paragraph as having taken place at a meeting at the police station in Ferizaj in the presence both of Mr. Mitic, the police chief, and Jashanin, possibly Ashanin, the DB representative in Ferizaj. You know nothing about this particular incident. Can I ask you whether you know of other similar cases?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Guy-Smith cross-examines, may I for the record indicate tab 13, which has been MFI'd as D172 is document identification 1D62-0010; tab 14, which has been MFI'd at D171 is document identification 1D62-0018; and tab 24 document id 1D63-0010 has not been identified as present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give you an -- Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith. Yes. Before I give you an opportunity to cross-examine the witness, Mr. Stijovic, I've got a more general question in relation to the last series of questions put to you by Mr. Emmerson. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber heard some evidence about the -- the origin of ammunition. The evidence - and I'm summarising now - is -- is that KLA used ammunition of Chinese origin but that the Serbian forces would also procure ammunition of Chinese origin. But the suggestion then, of course, was made that the use of this ammunition could suggest that what was achieved with this ammunition was KLA activity. Are you aware of any such thing that the origin of the ammunition played a role in activities, or did you ever come across such a thing in your intelligence activities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is just a serial type that the Kosovo Liberation Army was using Chinese-made ammunition. Whenever you mention China, it implies an old-fashioned weapons and ammunition. However, they used very modern weapons. As far as the State Security Service and the MUP is concerned, as per establishment and what was issued to me and other police officers, both in the public security sector and the state security sector, there was -- were no weapons that used Chinese ammunition. These weapons were for the most part produced by Zastava, which is in the Serbian town of Kragujevac, and the special units used, how to say, some more sophisticated weapons from the arsenal, such as Heckler & Koch and other weapons. So this is my general knowledge and I hope it was helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, your answer is limited to police officers, public security, and state security. Now, the Chamber also heard some evidence that sometimes there were combined operations. The Chamber also heard some evidence that sometimes by looking at the colour would look like army then changed from green/brown to blue, which then was meant to illustrate that these were police officers. Do you know anything about the use of Chinese ammunition in the broader sense of armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith. Yes, but before we continue, Mr. Emmerson, the registrar draws my attention to the fact that tab 24 has not been MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May it be MFI'd, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Guy-Smith --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption, Your Honours, but tab 24, that's document ID number 1D63-0010, will be marked for identification as D176.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Guy-Smith, you may proceed. Mr. Stijovic, Mr. Guy-Smith is counsel for -- Defence counsel for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to pick up in a general sense where we just left off, discussing the issue of special units. As I understand your testimony thus far, among other places that you received information, you also, as an intelligence analyst, received information concerning the special units that were operating throughout Kosovo. And I'll for the moment confine myself to the period from 1997 through to 1999. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. The analysis department in Pristina did not receive information or reports from units for special operations which was attached to the State Security Service, and even less from the SAJ, who were attached to the public security service. They had their own analysis department and were directly related to the service headquarters in Belgrade, both in terms of the line -- the chain of command and the analytics department line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you aware of a special unit whose name was Fog, who operated in Kosovo during the period of 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you from a document that has been identified as 2D758. It's the only document, I think that, we haven't put in the electronic disclosure system. We're attempting to -- the electronic system. We're attempting to use it, and we'll see what kind of success we can have. So if I can have that given to the Chamber as well as the Prosecution. I'd like to read something to you. This is from American RadioWorks, "Excerpts from interviews with militia members." And I'm specifically dealing with page 5 of that document. It's in English, so I will read it to you and see whether you can comment on this at all. "Predrag was a policeman in Pec. He joined a special police unit in early 1998. He says he participated in the attack in Cusaka on May 14th, 1999. Everyone had their fixed positions where they were supposed to hold. The Frenkies had its own. The Fog (OPG) had its own, the Yugoslav Army its own ... Fog went in first, or as we called them, 'the men in black'." Question: They wore black uniforms? Answer by Mr. Predrag: Yes, and the KLA wore black. So that was one of Fog's advantages against the KLA. They (Fog) went in first, to establish a bridge. We were on the wings ... We were on the left side. On the right side was Munja, the Pec boys. There was also a special police unit -- excuse me, that was also a special police unit. It wasn't paramilitary ... We made a wedge, then widened it." Do you have any information upon which you can comment concerning a group called Fog that wore black uniforms that were involved in military actions during 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will not hold this against me, but I'll do what I can to help you. I think it would exhibit a lack of seriousness on my part to comment upon a radio report. You asked me about Fog. This is the first time I hear of it. As for the OPG, yes, these are the so-called operations sweep groups that were part of special units of the MUP of Serbia. These were mobile groups which, in the event of a terrorist attack or action, were ready to act swiftly in that direction. You mentioned the Munja. I believe you said that they were Pec -- the Pec boys. We had a very serious problem, the State Security Service, with a person by the last name of Minic. He was a local criminal from Pec who used the nickname Munja and who was surrounded by several criminals. He took part in a number of events where those coming under attack from them were both Albanians and police officers. This was a criminal group. I took part in that action in 2001, where we tried to arrest them in Belgrade. However, the group -- or rather, the person managed to flee through illegal channels and the use of illegal papers and criminal channels. As far as I know, this person passed away in prison in Argentina at a later -- later date, later on. Now, as for who thought what and about who was where at a certain point in time, I don't think I should comment on that. This is what I can tell you on the basis of what you read out to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So if I -- if I understand your testimony correctly, with regard to Munja, this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you -- just for my information, we have been provided with a hard copy document, also American Radio works, but that's something different from --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: They gave you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what we have on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's differently different. It says: "Police units. And here it says: "Excerpts from interviews with militia members."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I must be -- I must be getting ahead of myself. Because that's the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's the next document I'm going to be using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I understand. But since you said it was not uploaded yet, I was a bit confused. But it's clear to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is why -- I'm trying to use our system. I'm trying to make it work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that also explains why I did not find anything on page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I understand your testimony correctly, you were aware of the fact that there was an organisation of criminals operating wearing black uniforms during the period of 1998 and 1999 in Kosovo who were engaged in attacking, as I understood your testimony, both Serbians as well as Albanian citizens; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
